title: Forces, Motion & Energy
description: Physics through play and experiment: pushes and pulls, magnets, light and shadow, sound, friction, gravity, energy transfer, electricity's relatives, and Newton's laws. Every concept is tested with hands-on investigations.

lessons.title: Push or Pull?
objectives: Sort actions into pushes and pulls
Notice that a bigger push makes something move more
explanation: To make something move, we push it or pull it. A push moves something away from you — like kicking a ball. A pull moves something towards you — like opening a drawer.
Pushes and pulls are called forces. A gentle push makes a toy car roll a little way. A strong push makes it roll further and faster.
Forces can also stop things moving or change their direction, like catching a ball or hitting it with a bat.

vocabulary.meaning: go from one place to another

examples: Pushing a swing.
Pulling a rope in tug of war.

story.title: The Stuck Cart
story.text: Momo's cart full of mangoes got stuck in the mud. Momo pulled from the front — it moved a little. Kiko pushed from behind — it moved a little more. "Together!" said Momo. Momo pulled and Kiko pushed at the same time, and the cart rolled free!

Tug of war uses…

How do you stop a rolling ball?
speaking: Show a grown-up three pushes and three pulls in your home and explain each.

assessment.prompt: Pulling a wagon moves it…

lessons.title: What Sticks to a Magnet?
objectives: Test which objects a magnet attracts
Know that magnets attract some metals but not all things
explanation: A magnet can pull some things towards it without touching them. We say the magnet attracts them.
Magnets attract things made of iron or steel, like paper clips and some spoons. They do not attract wood, plastic, paper or glass.
Not all metals are attracted! Coins, aluminium foil and copper are metals, but most of them are not attracted to a magnet.

vocabulary.meaning: an object that attracts iron and steel
a hard, shiny material like iron or steel

examples: A fridge magnet sticks to the steel fridge door.
A magnet does not pick up a wooden block.

story.title: Bolt's Magnet Hand
story.text: Bolt got a new magnet hand. It picked up paper clips — click! A spoon — clink! But when Bolt tried to pick up a banana, nothing happened. "Magnets only pull certain metals," explained Rangi. Bolt was a little disappointed — it had wanted a magnet banana.

activities.prompt: Which will a magnet pick up?

Magnets attract all metals.
activities.why: Most magnets attract iron and steel, not metals like aluminium or copper.

activities.prompt: "Attract" means…

lessons.title: Shadow Play
objectives: Name sources of light
Explain that a shadow forms when an object blocks light
explanation: We need light to see. Light comes from light sources like the Sun, lamps, torches and candles. The Moon is not a light source — it reflects the Sun's light.
Light travels in straight lines. When something blocks the light, it makes a dark shape behind it called a shadow.
Move closer to a torch and your shadow gets bigger. Move away and it gets smaller. Outside, shadows change length during the day as the Sun moves across the sky.

vocabulary.meaning: a dark shape made when light is blocked

examples: Your shadow is long in the morning and evening, short at midday.
Hand shadows can look like animals on a wall.

story.title: Kiko's Shadow Friend
story.text: Kiko kept seeing a dark goat following everywhere in the sunshine. "Who are you?" Kiko asked. It copied every move! Tara laughed: "That's your shadow. Your body blocks the sunlight." When a cloud covered the Sun, the shadow vanished. "Where did my friend go?" Kiko asked.

activities.prompt: Which is a light source?
A shadow forms when…

When is your shadow shortest outdoors?

thinking: Why don't we see shadows on a cloudy day?
Can you make a shadow with a glass of water? Why or why not?
speaking: Make hand shadow animals and explain how they are made.

lessons.title: Feel the Sound
objectives: Explain that sounds are made by vibrations
Describe sounds as loud/quiet and high/low
explanation: Every sound is made by something vibrating — moving back and forth very quickly. Touch your throat while humming: you can feel your voice box vibrating.
A harder hit makes bigger vibrations and a louder sound. A gentle tap makes a quieter sound.
Pitch is how high or low a sound is. A small, tight string makes a high sound; a long, loose string makes a low sound.

vocabulary.meaning: move back and forth very quickly
how high or low a sound is

examples: A drum skin vibrates when hit.
A bird's chirp is high pitch; a lion's roar is low pitch.

story.title: The Dancing Rice
story.text: Rangi put some rice grains on a drum and banged a pot nearby. The rice jumped and danced! "The sound makes the air shake, and the shaking air makes the drum shake," said Rangi. Quiet taps made tiny wiggles; loud bangs made the rice leap.

A harder hit on a drum makes the sound…

thinking: Why do you think we can't see most vibrations?
How could you make a guitar string sound higher?
speaking: Make a loud sound and a quiet sound with the same object, and explain the difference.

lessons.title: Slippery or Grippy?
objectives: Explain that friction is a force that slows moving things
Carry out a fair test on friction
explanation: Friction is a force between two surfaces rubbing together. It always works against movement, slowing things down.
Rough surfaces like carpet and sand have more friction. Smooth surfaces like ice and polished floors have less — that's why we slip.
Friction is useful: it lets our shoes grip, bicycle brakes stop us, and matches light. Sometimes we want less friction, so we use wheels, oil or smooth surfaces.

vocabulary.meaning: a force that slows things when surfaces rub
changing only one thing at a time

examples: Shoes with deep grooves grip better on wet ground.
Oil on a squeaky door hinge reduces friction.

story.title: The Great Slide Race
story.text: Momo, Kiko and Rangi raced down a slide wearing different clothes. Momo in woolly trousers stopped halfway. Kiko in shorts went a bit further. Rangi slid down on a smooth plastic mat and zoomed off the end! "Less friction, more speed," Rangi laughed.

activities.prompt: Which surface has the most friction?
Friction makes moving things…
Is friction helpful here?
In a fair test, we change only one thing.

thinking: What would happen if there were no friction at all?
Why do we put sand or grit on icy roads?
speaking: Explain to someone why you slip on a wet floor using the word friction.

assessment.prompt: To reduce friction in a machine we use…

lessons.title: Float or Sink?
objectives: Predict and test whether objects float or sink
Explain that shape affects floating
prerequisites: Understands forces as pushes and pulls
explanation: When you put something in water, gravity pulls it down and the water pushes it up. That upward push is called upthrust.
If the water can push up enough, the object floats. A cork, an apple and a leaf float. A stone, a coin and a key sink.
Shape matters! A ball of clay sinks, but the same clay shaped into a wide boat can float, because it pushes aside more water and gets more upthrust.

vocabulary.meaning: say what you think will happen

examples: Huge steel ships float because of their shape.
A coin sinks, but a cork floats.

story.title: Pala's Clay Boat Challenge
story.text: Pala the dolphin dared her friends: "Make clay float!" Kiko dropped a clay ball — plop, it sank. Rangi flattened the clay into a wide dish with sides. It bobbed on the water! They even loaded it with three pebbles before it sank.

activities.prompt: Which floats?
The water's upward push is called…
Changing the shape of clay can make it float.
Big steel ships float because of their…

thinking: Why do you think a huge ship floats but a tiny pebble sinks?
Do things float more easily in salty water? How could you find out?
speaking: Predict whether five objects will float or sink, test them, and explain any surprises.

assessment.prompt: Which sinks?

stages.overview: Forces and their effects, simple circuits of energy, and how light reflects and refracts.

units.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
units.summary: What happens when forces act together.
objectives: Draw force arrows to show size and direction

masteryCriteria: Uses newtons as the unit of force

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Force Arrows
objectives: Draw force arrows to show size and direction
Predict motion from balanced or unbalanced forces
explanation: We can draw forces as arrows. The arrow points in the direction of the force; a longer arrow means a bigger force. Forces are measured in newtons (N).
If the forces on an object are balanced — equal size, opposite directions — its motion does not change. A book resting on a table stays still; a car at steady speed keeps going.
If forces are unbalanced, the object speeds up, slows down or changes direction, in the direction of the bigger force.
examples: Tug of war with equal teams: balanced, no movement.
A parachute opening: air resistance greater than weight for a moment, so the skydiver slows down.

story.title: The Tug of War Draw
story.text: Heart Harbor's tug of war went on for ten minutes with the rope barely moving. "The forces are balanced!" Nova shouted. Then Momo joined the left team. The left team's force became bigger, and the rope zipped their way. "Unbalanced!" everyone laughed as the right team tumbled.

activities.prompt: Forces of 10 N left and 10 N right are…
15 N right and 5 N left. The object moves…
A car at steady speed in a straight line has balanced forces.
Force is measured in…

thinking: If forces are balanced, can an object still be moving? Explain.
Why does a ball rolling on grass eventually stop?
speaking: Draw force arrows on a picture of a cyclist and explain them to someone.

assessment.prompt: Unbalanced forces can make an object…
options: speed up, slow down or turn

assessment.prompt: A longer force arrow means…

assessment.why: Gravity pulls down and the table pushes up — balanced.

mastery: Uses newtons as the unit of force

lessons.title: Bounce and Bend
objectives: Explain how mirrors reflect light
Describe refraction and how a prism splits white light
prerequisites: Knows light travels in straight lines
explanation: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. A smooth mirror reflects light neatly: the angle the light hits at equals the angle it bounces off at.
Refraction is light bending when it passes from one material into another, like from air into water. That's why a straw in a glass of water looks bent.
White light is a mixture of colours. A prism refracts each colour by a slightly different amount, splitting light into a spectrum. Raindrops do the same to make rainbows.

context.text: Isaac Newton's prism experiments in the 1660s showed that white light is made of a spectrum of colours that can be recombined.

vocabulary.meaning: light bending as it passes into a different material
the band of colours in white light
a glass shape that splits light

examples: A periscope uses two mirrors to see over walls.
A swimming pool looks shallower than it is due to refraction.

story.title: Newton's Rainbow in a Room
story.text: In the 1660s, Isaac Newton darkened his room and let a thin beam of sunlight through a hole in the shutter. Passing it through a glass prism, he saw a band of colours on the wall. Then he used a second prism to recombine them into white light — proving the colours were in the sunlight all along.

activities.prompt: Match

project.safety: An adult should handle the glass and mirrors. Keep glass on a stable surface, never look directly at the Sun, and use the mirror only to view reflected light away from eyes.

units.title: Energy Stores and Transfers
units.summary: Energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred.
objectives: Identify energy stores and transfers in everyday situations
Apply the law of conservation of energy and calculate efficiency qualitatively
masteryCriteria: Identifies stores and transfers in systems

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Following the Energy
objectives: Identify energy stores and transfers in everyday situations
Apply the law of conservation of energy and calculate efficiency qualitatively
explanation: Energy is stored in different ways: kinetic (moving things), gravitational potential (raised objects), chemical (food, fuel, batteries), thermal (hot objects) and elastic (stretched springs).

Energy is transferred between stores by forces, heating, electricity, light and sound. When you eat breakfast and climb stairs, chemical energy is transferred to gravitational potential energy and some is transferred to thermal energy.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred (the law of conservation of energy). But some energy is usually "wasted", spreading out as heat or sound, so no machine is 100% efficient.

vocabulary.meaning: stored energy due to position or stretch
energy is never created or destroyed
useful energy out ÷ total energy in

examples: A falling ball: gravitational → kinetic.
A torch: chemical (battery) → electrical → light (useful) + heat (wasted).

story.title: The Bouncing Ball Mystery
story.text: Kiko dropped a ball from 1 metre. It bounced to 70 cm, then 50 cm, then lower each time until it stopped. "Where did the energy go?" Nova listened: each bounce made a sound and slightly warmed the ball and floor. "It didn't vanish," Nova said, "it spread out."

assessment.prompt: A ball at the top of a hill has mainly…

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Would You Weigh Less on the Moon?
objectives: Distinguish mass from weight
Calculate weight using W = m × g
prerequisites: Knows force is measured in newtons
explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere.
Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, measured in newtons. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g). On Earth, g ≈ 9.8 N/kg.
On the Moon, g ≈ 1.6 N/kg — about one-sixth of Earth's. A 30 kg child weighs about 294 N on Earth but only about 49 N on the Moon. Their mass is still 30 kg.

context.text: Surface gravity values: Earth ≈ 9.8 N/kg, Moon ≈ 1.6 N/kg, Mars ≈ 3.7 N/kg, Jupiter ≈ 24.8 N/kg (at cloud tops).

vocabulary.meaning: amount of matter, measured in kg
gravitational force on a mass, measured in N

examples: A 10 kg bag: weight ≈ 98 N on Earth.
Astronauts bounce on the Moon because of lower gravity.

story.title: Astronaut Bounces
story.text: When Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon in 1969–1972, they found that hopping was easier than walking. Their bodies and heavy suits had the same mass, but the Moon's weaker gravity pulled them down only about one-sixth as strongly.

goals: Apply Newton's three laws of motion

units.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
units.summary: The rules that govern how things move.
objectives: State and apply Newton's three laws
Calculate force, mass and acceleration
masteryCriteria: States and applies all three laws
Explains real phenomena with Newtonian reasoning

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: F = ma
objectives: State and apply Newton's three laws
Calculate force, mass and acceleration
explanation: First law: an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it (inertia). That's why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.
Second law: resultant force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). A 1000 kg car accelerating at 2 m/s² needs a resultant force of 2000 N.
Third law: when object A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. A rocket pushes gas backwards; the gas pushes the rocket forwards.

context.text: Newton published these laws in "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica" in 1687, building on work by Galileo and others.

examples: Seatbelts protect against inertia in a crash.
Swimming: you push water back, it pushes you forward.

story.title: The Tablecloth Trick
story.text: A magician whipped a tablecloth from under plates and cups — and they barely moved! It looked like magic, but it was Newton's first law. The cloth was pulled so quickly that friction acted only briefly, and the plates' inertia kept them in place.

activities.prompt: Match the law

A rocket moves forward because…
options: gas pushed backward pushes the rocket forward

activities.prompt: With no resultant force, a moving object keeps moving at constant velocity.

thinking: If action and reaction are equal, why doesn't everything cancel out and stay still?

speaking: Demonstrate each of Newton's laws using household objects and explain them.

assessment.prompt: Seatbelts are needed because of…

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Properties of Waves
objectives: Describe transverse and longitudinal waves
Use v = f × λ
explanation: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. In a transverse wave (light, water ripples), vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel. In a longitudinal wave (sound), vibrations are along the direction of travel.
Amplitude is the height of a wave (related to energy, loudness or brightness). Wavelength (λ) is the distance between peaks. Frequency (f) is how many waves pass per second, in hertz (Hz).
Wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = fλ). Sound in air travels at about 340 m/s; light in a vacuum at about 300,000,000 m/s.
examples: A 340 Hz sound in air has wavelength ≈ 1 m.
Seeing lightning before hearing thunder: light is far faster than sound.

story.title: Counting the Storm
story.text: During a storm, Zuri saw lightning and counted seconds until the thunder: three seconds. "Sound travels about 340 metres each second," she said, "so the lightning was about 1 kilometre away." Her little brother counted the next one: nine seconds — the storm was moving off.

activities.prompt: Match the wave to its type

Louder sound means bigger…

thinking: Why can't sound travel through space but light can?

speaking: Use a slinky or rope to demonstrate both wave types to someone and explain the difference.

project.title: Slinky and Water Wave Lab
steps: Make transverse and longitudinal waves on a slinky

assessment.prompt: Frequency is measured in…
